common_name: Love Pat Hosta (Thick-Leaved Rounded Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Love Pat forms a dense mound of thick, cupped leaves that takes a couple of seasons to fill out to full size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and avoid afternoon sun, which fades the blue leaf color. Registered in the late 1970s, Love Pat produces a tight, rounded mound of deeply cupped, heavily corrugated, powder-blue leaves with unusually thick substance for an older cultivar, and it has been used extensively as a breeding parent for many later blue and thick-leaved hosta introductions. Near-white flowers appear on short scapes in early summer, largely hidden beneath the foliage mound. The dense cupping and heavy leaf texture make it more resistant to slug damage than thinner-leaved hostas, though clumps are slow to divide and are best left undisturbed for several years to develop their full architectural form.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Piedmont Gold colors best with some morning sun and stays greener in deeper shade.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich soil in part shade, giving it enough morning sun to develop rich gold color without scorching the margins. Registered in the mid-1970s, Piedmont Gold was one of the first large gold-leaved hostas widely available in the American trade, producing a substantial mound of rounded, corrugated, chartreuse-to-gold leaves that hold their color well into summer. It has since been used as a parent in the breeding of numerous later gold and gold-margined hosta cultivars, making it historically significant beyond its own garden merit. Near-white flowers bloom on tall scapes above the foliage in midsummer, and mature clumps make a strong specimen or focal point in a partly shaded border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Blue Mammoth needs several years and generous spacing to reach its full mature spread.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing ample room since this is one of the largest blue-leaved hostas grown. Blue Mammoth forms an imposing clump of thick, heavily corrugated, sieboldiana-type blue-green leaves that hold their glaucous bloom well through the growing season, giving it strong slug resistance compared to thinner-leaved cultivars. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on stout scapes in early summer, though the plant is grown primarily as a foliage specimen. Because it takes five or more years to reach full size, site it where its eventual mass will not crowd smaller neighboring perennials.

common_name: Wolverine Hosta (Wide White-Margined Sport of June)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Wolverine is a vigorous grower that bulks up into a full clump faster than many variegated sports.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Wolverine is a sport of the popular cultivar 'June', retaining the blue-green leaf center but replacing June's gold-and-blue streaking with a broad, creamy-white-to-gold margin that gives the plant a bolder, more high-contrast look in the landscape. It is notably more vigorous and quicker to form a full-sized clump than its parent, making it useful where a fast-filling variegated groundcover effect is wanted. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, and occasional reverted shoots of solid green should be removed to keep the variegation consistent.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Golden Prayers develops its best gold color with a little morning sun and stays more compact than most gold hostas.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in part shade, giving a few hours of gentle morning light to intensify the gold foliage color. Golden Prayers shares its distinctive upright, vase-shaped growth habit and puckered, piecrust-edged leaves with its green-leaved sibling 'Praying Hands', but its foliage emerges and matures in bright chartreuse-gold rather than green, giving it a very different presence in the garden. The narrow, folded leaves stand nearly vertical rather than spreading into a typical mounded clump, making it a distinctive accent or edging plant in small spaces and containers. Near-white flowers appear on short scapes in summer above the compact foliage.

common_name: Hadspen Blue Hosta (Compact Tardiana Group Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hadspen Blue keeps its deepest blue color when grown in fairly deep shade away from afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade to preserve the waxy blue bloom on the leaf surface, which sun exposure gradually strips away. Hadspen Blue came out of the Tardiana group of hostas bred in England from crosses involving Hosta sieboldiana 'Elegans', and it forms a compact, rounded mound of small, thick, intensely blue-gray leaves noticeably smaller and neater than many of its Tardiana relatives. Its dense, low habit suits it to the front of a shade border or a container planting where a larger blue hosta would be out of scale. Near-white to pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, and the thick leaves offer good resistance to slug feeding.

common_name: Jurassic Park Hosta (Giant Corrugated Blue-Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jurassic Park needs several years and 5–7 feet of clearance in every direction to reach full size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, reserving a large open area since this cultivar becomes one of the largest hostas commonly available. Jurassic Park produces enormous, deeply corrugated, blue-green leaves on a clump that expands steadily for years before reaching its full massive proportions, making it a slow long-term investment rather than a quick-filling plant. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall, sturdy scapes well above the foliage mass in summer. Because of its eventual size, it works best as a single specimen or anchor plant in a large shaded bed rather than in a mixed border of smaller perennials.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Total Eclipse develops its darkest color in deeper shade, since bright light bleaches the dark pigment.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade to keep the leaf color as dark as possible, since sun exposure fades the near-black pigment toward ordinary blue-green. Total Eclipse produces thick, rounded, heavily corrugated leaves in one of the darkest shades available among hosta cultivars, giving it striking value as a contrast plant against gold- or white-variegated companions in a shade planting. Near-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the foliage color is the main attraction. Its thick leaf substance also provides above-average resistance to slug damage compared with thinner green cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Aztec Treasure tolerates more morning sun than many gold hostas without scorching, which helps deepen its color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in part shade, allowing some morning sun to bring out the fullest gold tone in the foliage. Aztec Treasure forms an upright, vase-shaped clump of thick, rounded, glossy gold-yellow leaves that hold their color and substance well through summer heat better than many older gold cultivars. White flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in midsummer. The plant's above-average sun tolerance and clean, bright color make it a useful gold accent for shade borders that get a bit more light than the deep shade preferred by blue-leaved hostas.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Twist of Lime holds its gold center best with a bit of morning sun and keeps its narrow, twisted leaf form best in a spot sheltered from strong wind.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade, sheltered from strong wind that can tatter its narrow foliage. Twist of Lime is grown for its distinctive leaf shape rather than a typical hosta form: narrow, elongated, lance-shaped leaves with a bright gold-yellow center and dark green margin twist gently along their length, giving the clump a lively, textural look unlike the broad rounded leaves of most cultivars. Lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its small stature and unusual form make it a good textural accent among broader-leaved hostas or paired with ferns and heucheras in a mixed shade planting.
